Changed travel plans lead into an explanation of shared work

Paul had planned two visits and did not come (verses 15–16). Verse 17 shows the charge he expects: that he plans lightly. Verse 23 gives his reason under oath: he stayed away to spare them. That could sound like a ruler holding back punishment. Verse 24 corrects it at once. He does not control their faith. He is a fellow worker for their joy, and they stand by faith.
Sufficient punishment must give way to comfort and restored love

Verse 6 says the majority punished the man, and that it is sufficient. Paul does not say the punishment was wrong. Verse 7 says what must come next: forgiveness and comfort. The reason is the man himself. Too much sorrow could swallow him up. Verse 8 asks them to confirm their love for him. Verse 11 adds a second reason: Satan must gain no advantage.
The believers themselves become the letter Paul offers as evidence

Verse 1 raises the matter of letters of recommendation. Some carry them to Corinth or from Corinth. Verse 2 says Paul’s letter is the Corinthians themselves. Verse 3 names the author, the carrier, and the material. Christ wrote it, Paul delivered it, and the Spirit was the ink. It is written on hearts and not on stone tablets. That contrast with stone opens the comparison with Moses in verses 7–11.
Fragile carriers keep the power distinct from the people carrying it

Verse 6 describes a treasure: the light of God’s glory in Christ’s face. Verse 7 says where it is kept: in clay vessels. Clay breaks easily, and verses 8–9 list the blows. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down. The verse gives the purpose of the weak container. The great power must be seen as God’s and not Paul’s. Verse 10 says Jesus’ life shows in a body that carries his death.
Restored relationship changes the way Paul sees and addresses others

Verse 17 says anyone in Christ is a new creation. Verse 18 says where that comes from: “all things are of God.” God did the reconciling, through Christ. The same verse gives Paul his task, the service of reconciliation. Verse 19 explains it: God does not count their trespasses against them. Verse 20 shows how the task sounds: an ambassador who begs. Paul speaks for Christ and asks them to be reconciled to God.
An open heart stands beside a warning about divided belonging

Verses 4–10 list what Paul has borne for his work. Verse 11 then turns to the readers by name: “Corinthians.” His mouth is open and his heart is wide. Verse 12 says the tightness is on their side. Verse 13 asks for a fair return, and he speaks as to children. The same request comes back in 7:2: “Open your hearts to us.”
Paul values grief through its changed response rather than its pain alone

Verse 8 admits the letter hurt them and Paul regretted it briefly. Verse 9 says exactly what he is glad about. It is not their pain. It is that the pain led to repentance. Verse 10 separates two sorrows: one leads to salvation and one to death. Verse 11 lists what theirs produced: eagerness, indignation, fear, longing, and zeal. By that result Paul judges the grief good.
Willing giving must use available means without transferring distress

Paul has just praised the Macedonians for giving beyond their means (verse 3). Verse 12 keeps that from becoming a demand. A gift is measured by what one has, not by what one lacks. Verse 13 states the aim in a negative. Others are not to be eased while Corinth is pressed. Verse 14 gives the aim: plenty on one side meets need on the other. Verse 15 quotes the manna: no one had too much or too little.
Advance preparation protects a gift from pressure and shame

Verses 3–5 explain why brothers come ahead of Paul. The gift should be ready as a blessing and not as a forced payment. Verse 7 gives the rule behind that care. Each gives what he has decided in his own heart. Two things are ruled out: reluctance and compulsion. The reason is in the verse: God loves a cheerful giver. Verse 8 answers the fear behind reluctance: God can supply enough.
Authority must build the hearers rather than merely win a comparison

Verse 10 quotes Paul’s critics: strong letters, weak presence. He must defend his authority and not merely boast. Verse 8 does it by naming the purpose of the authority. The Lord gave it for building them up, not for casting them down. So he can speak of it without shame. Verse 9 adds that he does not mean to frighten them by letters. The same words about building up return in 13:10.
Forced boasting becomes a record of weakness and care

Verse 18 says many boast according to the flesh, so Paul will too. Verses 22–23 match his rivals: Hebrew, Israelite, servant of Christ. Then the list changes direction. From verse 23 he counts beatings, stonings, and shipwrecks, not successes. Verse 29 asks who is weak without his being weak. Verse 30 states the rule he has followed: he boasts in his weakness. The last item fits it: he left Damascus lowered in a basket (verse 33).
The remembered answer redirects boasting toward grace within weakness

Verse 7 says the thorn was given to keep Paul from being lifted up. Verse 8 says he asked three times for it to leave. Verse 9 is the answer, and the thorn stays. The Lord gives grace instead and a reason: power is made perfect in weakness. Paul’s response is in the same verse. He will gladly boast in weaknesses, so that Christ’s power rests on him. Verse 10 sums it up: when he is weak, then he is strong.
A final warning aims to make harsh action unnecessary

Verse 2 warns that Paul will not spare anyone when he comes. Verse 10 explains why he writes it first. A letter gives time to change before he arrives. Then he will not need to deal sharply. The verse also repeats the limit on his authority from 10:8. The Lord gave it for building up and not for tearing down. Verse 9 shows what he wants: their being made complete.
